transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi. Yes, thank you. Well, I'm here because... I just can't stop seeing this terrible droop and unevenness around my mouth and my jaw. It's in every photo, every single reflection. Actually, my firm just redid our website and they made us all take new headshots, and the photographer used this incredibly harsh overhead lighting. It’s exactly the kind of lighting I tell my architecture clients to avoid in their kitchens because it casts the absolute worst shadows. Just last Tuesday I had a client who insisted on these awful industrial pendant lights, and I spent an hour trying to explain light diffusion to him, but people just don't listen when they have a Pinterest board in their head, you know? 

But... anyway, what was I saying? Right, my jaw. Even when my husband or people at work tell me I look fine, I know they're just being polite. It feels so glaringly obvious to me. It's gotten so bad that I’ve actually started avoiding my presentations and getting out of meeting with clients entirely. I just can't stand the thought of them staring at my mouth.
How long have you been feeling this way about your appearance, and have you noticed any other changes in your mood or energy levels during this time?

How long... gosh, I really couldn't give you an exact timeframe. I'm not sure. Time has just been so strange lately anyway. We just finished this massive commercial build downtown—the one with the big glass atrium on 4th street?—and that project took almost three years, but honestly it felt like three months. The permitting process in this city is just a complete nightmare right now. I was down at the zoning office for, well, it had to be four hours last Thursday, just waiting. And the clerk working the desk had this incredibly asymmetrical haircut. I couldn't tell if it was an intentional stylistic choice or just a terrible mistake, but it completely threw off the visual balance of her face. Visual balance is just... it's everything. If a foundation is off by even a fraction of an inch, the whole structure suffers, you know? 

But... I'm sorry, what were you asking? Something about my energy? I haven't really noticed any changes with my mood or energy, if that's what you mean. I haven't really kept track of that. Just... I don't know. I'm not sure.

Do you find yourself doing anything repeatedly—like checking mirrors, adjusting your face, or seeking reassurance—to try to fix or make sure others don’t notice the asymmetry around your mouth and jaw?

Well, yes, I... I do. Before work or, really, before any family event, I can spend hours just checking the bathroom mirror. I'll take pictures on my phone from every possible angle, trying to figure out how bad it is. And I'll redo my makeup, adjust my scarf, ask my husband over and over if my face looks lopsided... which, honestly, he's a saint for putting up with it. He's been so patient, especially lately. We just had our 25th anniversary, actually. We were supposed to go to Italy—I had this whole itinerary planned out, focusing on Renaissance architecture, obviously. Brunelleschi's dome in Florence, I mean, the structural ingenuity of it is just staggering when you consider the technology they had at the time. They didn't even use scaffolding! Can you imagine trying to get a permit for that today? The inspectors would have a field day. 

But... oh, right. The checking. Yeah, I do all of that, and then I end up just scrolling through photos of other women online, trying to see how awful my jaw looks compared to theirs. It's just exhausting.
Has this concern about your jaw and mouth affected your personal life or relationships, like spending less time with friends or family, or avoiding social events altogether?

Yes, it really has. It's... it's ruining everything, honestly. I just cancelled a major client presentation at the very last minute. I was supposed to present the final renderings for a boutique hotel lobby, and I just couldn't do it. I couldn't stand the thought of them all sitting around that long conference table, just staring at my face while I talked. Which is a shame, because the renderings were beautiful. We sourced this incredible reclaimed wood from a barn in upstate New York for the reception desk. The grain on it is just spectacular. It has so much character, you know? Not like that cheap veneer everyone uses now. My contractor was complaining about how hard it is to work with, but I told him, you can't rush craftsmanship. 

But... wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, the presentation. Yeah, I cancelled it, and I've been skipping all these networking events for an industry award we're up for. I just can't face being seen. And because I'm hiding out so much, my project deadlines are slipping, and I've even stopped going to family gatherings. Everything is just starting to fall apart because I can't let people see my face.
